name: world feature
description: Land, water and other large things an open world is made of: terrain tiles, mountains, islands, coasts, seas, lakes, rivers, biomes and settlements.
conventions: World pieces are built in tiles (chunks) so they can be streamed in and out: a tile is typically 64-1024 m wide.
y = 0 is sea level. Land is above it, a sea floor is below it. Heights are in metres, never a 0-1 range baked into the mesh.
A tile's origin is the centre of its footprint at y = 0, so neighbouring tiles line up at whole multiples of the tile size.
Neighbouring tiles share their border vertices with exactly the same heights, or cracks open between them.
A heightmap tile has a power of two plus one vertices per side (65, 129, 257, 513), so the last row of one tile is the first row of the next.
anticipate: Collision from the same heights: a HeightMapShape3D takes map_width x map_depth floats in map_data (or update_map_data_from_image), instead of a trimesh of the whole surface.
Levels of detail by distance: GeometryInstance3D visibility_range_begin and visibility_range_end switch tiles or detail meshes, and a coarser edge row needs a skirt or stitching so it does not crack.
Scatter (trees, rocks, grass) as MultiMesh instances placed from the terrain heights, not one node per object.
A big world loses float precision far from the origin: recentre the world around the player (floating origin) or use a double-precision Godot build.
pitfalls: Stretched textures on steep slopes: a top-down UV smears on cliffs, so blend a triplanar or a second texture by slope.
A coast that ends at y = 0 with a sharp edge: let the land slope below sea level so the shore line has depth to show.
One huge mesh for the whole world: it cannot be culled or streamed. Cut it into tiles.

name: terrain
description: A landscape surface: a heightmap tile or a larger piece of ground.

parts.name: Surface
parts.note: The ground mesh: a grid of height samples, with a normal and a UV per vertex.

parts.name: Collision
parts.note: A StaticBody3D with a HeightMapShape3D built from the same heights as the surface.

scale.source: general knowledge: usual tile sizes in open-world engines (64-1024 m); the height range depends on the landscape: plains a few metres, mountains hundreds to thousands

anticipate: A splat or slope-based material (grass, rock, sand, snow) instead of one texture over the whole tile.
pitfalls: Noise-only terrain looks the same everywhere: combine large smooth shapes (domain) with a ridged or fractal detail layer, and flatten where roads and buildings go.

name: mountain
description: A mountain, a mountain range or a volcano.

scale.source: general knowledge: a hill is a few tens to hundreds of metres, a mountain from about 300 m up to 4-6 km in most ranges; the highest point on Earth is about 8,849 m above sea level

pitfalls: A cone with uniform slopes looks like a pile of sand: add ridged noise, a few steep faces and scree at the foot.

name: island
description: An island or a group of islands.

parts.name: SeaFloor
parts.note: The land keeps sloping down below y = 0 for tens of metres so the water has depth around the shore.

scale.source: general knowledge: from a sandbank of a few metres high to volcanic islands over 1 km high; length and width are the extent of the land above the water

conventions: The coastline is the y = 0 contour of the heightmap: the sea plane sits at y = 0 and the land crosses it.

name: coast
description: A stretch of coast: beach, dunes, cliffs or a harbour edge where land meets water.

parts.name: Shoreline
parts.note: Where the surface crosses y = 0; a foam or wet-sand band can follow it.

scale.source: general knowledge: a coast segment is as long as you choose; dunes are 5-30 m high, sea cliffs from a few metres to over 200 m

pitfalls: A straight coast looks artificial: bend it with large and small bays, and make cliffs and beaches alternate.

name: body of water
description: A sea, lake or river: a water surface with a floor and shores.

parts.name: Surface
parts.note: A flat, subdivided plane at the water level; waves come from a vertex shader and a normal map, not from modelled geometry.

parts.name: Floor
parts.note: The ground under the water, which should slope smoothly down from the shore.

anticipate: A subdivided PlaneMesh (subdivide_width and subdivide_depth) for a surface that has vertex waves, and a ShaderMaterial for depth colour, foam and refraction.
A function that returns the water height at a position, so boats and floating things can follow the waves.
A water volume (Area3D) for swimming and drag, separate from the visual surface.
pitfalls: Modelling waves in geometry: it costs triangles and cannot move; use a shader.
A water plane that ends in the view: make it follow the camera or extend it far beyond the visible area.

name: sea

scale.source: general knowledge: shelf seas are 0-200 m deep (the North Sea averages about 95 m); the visible plane is as large as the view needs

conventions: The sea surface is at y = 0; the sea floor is below it.
pitfalls: A single plane for the whole sea cannot be as large as the world and detailed near the camera: use a plane that follows the camera with finer rings close by.

name: lake
description: A lake, pond or other still inland water.

scale.source: general knowledge: ponds are a few metres deep, large lakes tens to hundreds of metres

conventions: A lake's surface is flat at its own height, not at y = 0; place it in a basin that is lower than its whole shoreline.
pitfalls: A lake whose shore is lower than the water on one side: the water would run out. Check the lowest point of the rim.

name: river

parts.name: Surface
parts.note: A strip that follows the river's path and flows downhill; its UV should scroll along the flow.

parts.name: Bed
parts.note: A channel carved into the terrain along the same path.

scale.source: general knowledge: a segment is as long as you choose; streams are 1-5 m wide, big rivers hundreds of metres, depth from a few decimetres to tens of metres

conventions: A river always flows downhill: its surface height falls along the path, in small steps if the water is a series of flat pieces.
pitfalls: A river that runs uphill or over a ridge: carve the channel into the terrain along the path instead of drawing a strip over it.

name: biome
description: A region with its own ground, plants and mood: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, swamp or jungle.

parts.name: Ground
parts.note: The ground material for this region: grass, sand, rock, snow, mud.

parts.name: Vegetation
parts.note: MultiMesh scatter of trees, bushes and grass placed from a density map.

parts.name: Props
parts.note: Rocks, logs and other small things that make the region feel lived in.

scale.source: general knowledge: a biome region is as large as the design needs; tiles of 100 m to a few km are blended at the borders

anticipate: Smooth borders: blend ground materials and thin out the plants over tens of metres instead of a hard line.
pitfalls: Every tree the same size and rotation: vary scale (80-120%), rotation and tint per instance.

name: settlement
description: A village, town or city placed in the world.

parts.name: Buildings
parts.note: Instances of a few building types, placed along the roads and rotated to face them.

parts.name: Landmark
parts.note: A church, tower or square that gives the place a recognisable centre.

scale.source: general knowledge: a hamlet is about 100 m across, a village a few hundred metres, a town a few km

anticipate: Flatten the terrain under roads and buildings so they sit on the ground instead of floating or sinking.
Collision on the roads and a navigation region over the walkable areas.
pitfalls: Streets on a perfect grid look artificial: bend them, vary the plot sizes and let them follow the slope.
